title: Tamsin and the Trembling Bridge
markdown:
Sunlight blasted through Tamsin’s window in gold stripes that painted her face as if the day had already picked a side. Birds started up like a workshop of small machines. She bounced out of bed with her inventive mind already halfway to the creek. Today the town would inspect the Willow Creek footbridge at noon. Dad had said the words last night over toast, casual as weather, and they had sat in her chest all night like a bolt that needed a turn.

Birch, her scruffy scrapyard dog, thumped his tail against the bedframe. “Morning, big guy,” Tamsin said. “Ready?” Birch barked, a sound that promised he was already ahead of her.

They dashed out. Dew still clung to the grass. Then a familiar sound cut the morning: RATTLE-CLATTER-WHINE. The footbridge. Her greatest unfinished argument with metal. A tremor of worry went through her, practical as a checklist. The inspectors liked still bridges. This one liked to sing.

They trotted to the creek. Dewdrops caught the light. The boards groaned and shook in the wind. Birch sniffed, tail ticking. Tamsin tugged a rail. Pushed a post. Shook the whole span as if it might confess. Nothing budged that she wanted to budge. Frustration rose, hot and useless. Birch whined and would not leave a patch of ivy.

“What have you found?” She sighed and went over. He nudged the greenery. She pulled. Fingertips met something hard, metallic, forgotten. The ivy tore and showed a bracket almost swallowed by leaves: a vital support, loose as a rumour.

“Brilliant, Birch.” Relief arrived too early. She took her multi-tool, the one with the nicked grip, and set to work. A quick tighten. A firm twist. She stepped back, hopeful as a first draft.

RATTLE-CLATTER-WHINE. Louder, if anything, as if the bridge had opinions about being half-fixed.

Tamsin’s shoulders slumped. Noon was a bright coin already sliding down the sky. “Maybe I should tell Dad it’s impossible,” she muttered. The words tasted like quitting. Birch whined softly and nudged her hand, then scanned the railing with the patience of a dog who had found one secret and expected another. His gaze flicked to a small, almost invisible nut.

She followed. A crucial bolt, the one that joined the bracket to the main support, sat a hair loose. The first repair had been a hat on a problem that still had a head.

“Of course.” Her voice came back. This was the real work. She had to reach it. She jammed her arm into the thorny ivy, ignored the pricks, and braced. A scratch opened on her cheek as she leaned. She shut her eyes, held her breath, and twisted. The tool slipped once, bit again. A decisive click. A last firm turn that travelled up her wrist.

The bridge stood still.

Silent.

Not a holy silence. An engineering one: wood and iron agreeing, for now, to be a path. Water talked underneath, ordinary as always. Tamsin grinned so wide it pulled the scratch. She, trainee engineer, with Birch the scrapyard finder, had tamed the rattle.

She wiped the tool on her jeans, checked the nut once more because Dad would, and rested her palm on the rail. No shiver. Birch sat, proud and muddy, as if he had tightened it with his nose.

“Today,” she told him, quieter than a declaration and twice as sure, “is going to be a good one.”

They did not race off in a blur. They walked the span end to end, counting boards, listening. Noon would come with clipboards. The bridge, at last, had nothing extra to say. Birch’s tail made the only rattle left, and Tamsin let it.
